blocks.text: HCC is the **commonest primary liver tumour** and makes up over 80% of primary liver cancers. Davidson ranks it the sixth most frequent cancer worldwide. **Cirrhosis is present in 75–90%** of patients and is the main risk factor. HCC is commoner in **men** and risk rises with **age**: about half of UK cases present after 65.

blocks.title: Risk factors for HCC
rows: Hepatitis B; hepatitis C; HBV/HDV co-infection
HBV raises risk about 100-fold and is the leading cause worldwide. HIV co-infection with HCV raises fibrosis and HCC risk
Alcohol, NASH/NAFLD, haemochromatosis, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, Wilson disease
Each cirrhosis cause carries extra risk; viral cirrhosis risk is 1–5%
Aflatoxin (from _Aspergillus flavus_ growing on groundnuts), vinyl chloride, tobacco
Aflatoxin is the classic environmental carcinogen
Androgenic (anabolic) steroids; oral contraceptive pill (weak link)
Same drugs are linked to hepatic adenoma
Diabetes, autoimmune hepatitis, schistosomiasis, type 1 glycogen storage disease, hepatic adenoma

blocks.title: Hepatitis B versus hepatitis C
items: **HBV inserts its DNA into the hepatocyte genome**, so it can cause HCC **without cirrhosis**
About 90% of HCC patients in northern Europe have cirrhosis, compared with only 30% in Taiwan, where HBV is the main cause
HBV annual HCC risk: **0.4% without cirrhosis, 2–6% with cirrhosis**, and about **4× higher if HBeAg-positive**
HCV does not integrate into host DNA. Per Kumar, HCV-related HCC arises on a cirrhotic liver
Mass **HBV vaccination** has lowered HCC incidence in high-prevalence countries such as Taiwan, where HBV is mostly acquired perinatally

blocks.text: In **hereditary haemochromatosis with cirrhosis**, HCC is the leading cause of death and affects about one-third of patients. Venesection lowers the risk but does not remove it, so **surveillance must continue** even after iron stores return to normal.

Two kinds of risk get mixed up. Davidson calls **HBV the major risk factor worldwide** (global burden). Kumar says an individual **HCV carrier has a higher risk than an HBV carrier**, and co-infection carries the highest risk. Also, **absent cirrhosis does not exclude HCC in HBV**.

HCC reaches the clinic by one of **two routes**. (1) **Decompensation** of cirrhosis that is known or was never diagnosed: worsening ascites, jaundice or variceal bleeding, often with weight loss, anorexia and abdominal pain. Disease found this way is usually **too advanced to cure**. (2) **Surveillance** of at-risk patients picks up smaller, asymptomatic tumours, which leaves more treatment options. Surveillance finds a growing share of cases.

blocks.title: Symptoms and signs
items: Constitutional: **weight loss, anorexia, fever**, fatigue, nausea and vomiting
Right upper quadrant ache; **enlarged, irregular, tender liver** or a right hypochondrial mass
**Hepatic bruit** from the vascular tumour; **rupture** can cause intra-abdominal bleeding
Features of chronic liver disease: **ascites, jaundice**, pruritus, splenomegaly, encephalopathy
Liver cancer is often silent for a long time and presents late

blocks.title: Paraneoplastic features
items: **Erythrocytosis**: HCC is on the classic list with renal cell carcinoma and cerebellar haemangioblastoma
**Hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia**, hypercholesterolaemia
Thrombocytosis (rare), carcinoid syndrome, hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy
By contrast, a **low** platelet count usually points to the underlying chronic liver disease

blocks.title: How it spreads
items: Blood supply comes mainly from the **hepatic artery**, which is what TACE exploits
Spreads by **invading the portal vein** and its branches
Davidson: lymph node metastases common; lung and bone metastases rare

blocks.text: Classic exam stem: a **cirrhotic patient who deteriorates quickly** with weight loss, RUQ pain and ascites, or who has a **palpable liver mass with a raised AFP**, has HCC until proven otherwise. In cirrhosis, any new focal liver lesion is very likely to be HCC.
A patient with no known liver disease can still have HCC on cirrhosis. The tumour-driven decompensation is often the event that **first reveals hidden cirrhosis**.

**Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)** is the tumour marker for HCC. Davidson: about **60% of HCCs produce AFP**. Levels climb with tumour size, so small tumours found by screening often have a normal or only slightly raised AFP. Kumar and KC Essentials: AFP is **normal in at least one-third** of patients.

blocks.title: Interpreting serum AFP
rows: > 400 ng/mL (330 IU/mL) or rising on serial tests, without a hepatitis flare
Tracks progression or response to treatment
Non-seminomatous germ cell tumour of the gonad
The other tumour that raises AFP

blocks.title: Other blood tests
items: Liver biochemistry, full blood count, creatinine and electrolytes
Coagulation, albumin: coagulopathy and low albumin show how much liver function is left
**Hepatitis B and C serology** to identify the cause
**CA19-9** is the marker for cholangiocarcinoma, not HCC

blocks.title: Surveillance (screening)
items: **Ultrasound plus AFP every 6 months** for high-risk patients fit enough to be treated
Who: cirrhosis from HBV, HCV, haemochromatosis, alcohol, NASH or α1-antitrypsin deficiency, **plus chronic HBV even without cirrhosis**
Pocket Medicine: MRI may alternate with ultrasound in the highest-risk patients
A new lesion or a rising AFP leads to **three-phase contrast CT or MRI**
Screening detects smaller tumours, often < 3 cm, which are more likely to be curable

blocks.text: **A normal AFP does not exclude HCC.** AFP has low sensitivity and specificity, and small tumours are often AFP-negative. The books give different figures (Davidson: 60% secrete it; Step-Up: raised in 40–70%; Kumar: normal in ≥ one-third). Use Davidson’s figure.

blocks.title: Imaging in suspected HCC
rows: First-line and screening test; shows filling defects in ~90%, portal vein involvement and signs of cirrhosis
Detects lesions down to about 2–3 cm; very operator-dependent (contrast agents help)
HCC is **hypervascular**: it enhances in the arterial phase, then **washes out** in portal venous/delayed phases
Small nodules are hard to separate from regenerative nodules
Characterises small or uncertain lesions; alternative to CT
Now used for therapy (embolisation of vascular tumours)
Rarely used for diagnosis now; replaced by CT/MRI

blocks.title: Imaging rules
items: Use **at least two modalities** to diagnose and stage, usually CT or MRI after a screening ultrasound finds a mass
In high-risk patients, the typical three-phase CT/MRI pattern establishes HCC **without biopsy**

blocks.note: Look at: a large hepatocellular carcinoma on contrast CT (arrows).
Look at: arterial-phase enhancement, then washout on portal venous and delayed phases, on both CT and MRI.

blocks.title: Liver biopsy: when and when not
items: **Advisable**: a large tumour in a patient **without cirrhosis or HBV**, to confirm HCC and exclude a metastasis
Otherwise only when imaging is **equivocal**; non-invasive diagnosis is preferred
**Avoid** in possible resection or transplant candidates: **needle-tract seeding** risk (< 2%)
Other risks: bleeding, pneumothorax, and sampling error giving a false negative
Ask whether the result would change management before weighing it against bleeding risk
Histology: tumour cells resemble hepatocytes; well-differentiated HCC can look almost like normal liver

blocks.note: Look at: H&E histology of HCC, with tumour cells that resemble hepatocytes.

blocks.text: KC Essentials: in a cirrhotic liver, a mass **> 2 cm** is almost certainly HCC and **biopsy is not indicated**.

The books disagree on the size below which a CT lesion is hard to characterise: **Davidson < 2 cm** (versus regenerative nodules) and Kumar < 1 cm. Use Davidson’s 2 cm, and use MRI for small indeterminate nodules.

sections.title: Differential diagnosis of focal liver lesions

blocks.text: Approach to a liver mass: **first establish whether chronic liver disease is present** and how severe it is, because the differential changes completely. In cirrhosis a new lesion is probably HCC. Overall, **metastases are the commonest malignant liver lesion** (Pocket Medicine: only about 15% of liver masses are HCC), and **benign lesions are frequent**. Use several imaging modalities.

blocks.title: Focal liver lesions compared
rows: Known or occult primary (GI tract, breast, lung, pelvis)
Usually multiple; **ALP is the commonest abnormality** (LFTs may be normal); filling defects on CT
Find the primary; resect selected (e.g. colorectal) metastases
Adolescent or young adult, either sex
No HBV or cirrhosis; large; **AFP usually normal**; tumour cells in dense fibrous stroma
Not linked to cirrhosis or HBV; jaundice and cholangitis more common than in HCC; CA19-9
Commonest benign tumour; usually < 5 cm, asymptomatic; CT: low density with delayed arterial filling
Up to 10 cm; **central scar** on CT/MRI; no malignant potential
Woman on the **oral contraceptive pill**; androgen/anabolic steroid users
May grow in pregnancy and **rupture** (intraperitoneal bleed)
Resect if symptomatic, > 5 cm or no shrinkage after stopping the pill

blocks.note: Look at: multiple liver metastases on CT, which are numerous and scattered, unlike a single dominant HCC.
Look at: a haemangioma on MRI (arrows).
Look at: multiple cysts in both liver and kidneys in polycystic disease.

blocks.text: **Fibrolamellar HCC** is a different disease from ordinary HCC. Think of it for a **young patient with a big liver mass, a normal AFP and no liver disease**. It has a much better prognosis after resection.

The books disagree on **FNH and oestrogen**. Zero to Finals links FNH to oestrogen/the pill; Step-Up says there is no association; Davidson mentions only that FNH is common in women under 40. The lesion **clearly tied to the pill, and the one that ruptures, is the hepatic adenoma**.
Adenoma malignant potential: Step-Up quotes about a **10% transformation risk**, and Kumar notes it is **much higher in men**. Davidson gives no figure.

sections.title: Staging and surgery: resection and transplantation

blocks.text: Management differs **with and without cirrhosis**. In cirrhosis, treatment depends on **tumour size and number, liver function (Child–Pugh) and performance status**. Prognosis depends on size, **vascular invasion** and liver function. Overall median survival is only about 6–20 months; unresectable disease usually kills within a year.

blocks.title: Resection versus transplantation
rows: **Non-cirrhotic liver** (treatment of choice); in cirrhosis only small tumours with **Child–Pugh A and no portal hypertension**
Cirrhosis with tumour within the **Milan criteria**: **one lesion < 5 cm, or up to three each < 3 cm**
Inadequate liver reserve (risk of hepatic failure)
About 50% 5-year survival, but about 50% recur within 5 years
The remaining cirrhotic liver can grow new tumours
Cures the cirrhosis and removes de novo risk; immunosuppression may speed up residual tumour; hepatitis C can recur in the graft

blocks.title: Transplant referral facts
items: HCC **< 5 cm** in cirrhosis is an indication to refer for transplant assessment
UK listing (category 2): HCC shown by **two concordant imaging modalities**, within the Milan-type size limits, with **no macrovascular invasion or metastases**
About 11% of liver transplants in Europe and the USA are for HCC
Pocket Medicine (US): evaluate at MELD ≥ 15; HCC earns exception points
Only about 10% of patients have resectable tumours

blocks.text: For a **small primary in a cirrhotic liver**, transplantation is the only treatment that offers a real chance of cure, because it removes the whole at-risk liver.
Survival after resection is quoted differently: **Davidson ~50% at 5 years** (non-cirrhotic) versus Step-Up 25%. Use Davidson’s figure.

sections.title: Ablation, chemoembolisation, systemic and supportive therapy

blocks.title: Stage-based algorithm for HCC in cirrhosis (Davidson Fig. 22.36, EASL–EORTC/BCLC)
rows: Single < 2 cm, or single < 5 cm, or 3 nodules < 3 cm; PST 0, Child–Pugh A
Single + normal portal pressure → **resection**; raised portal pressure or 3 nodules → **transplant** (no other illness) or **RFA/PEI** (other illness)
Portal vein invasion, N1 or M1, PST 1–2

blocks.note: Look at: the staging algorithm that links tumour burden, performance status and Child–Pugh score to each treatment.

blocks.title: Local ablation
items: **Percutaneous ethanol (alcohol) injection** under ultrasound: about **80% cure for tumours ≤ 3 cm**; recurrence about 50% at 3 years, similar to resection
**Radiofrequency ablation**: one electrode placed under imaging; takes longer but may destroy more of the tumour
KC Essentials also mentions high-frequency ultrasound probes; Pocket and Kumar add stereotactic body radiotherapy
**Cryotherapy/cryoablation** and thermal ablation: Kumar lists them as local options for liver metastases. The books give no HCC-specific data

blocks.title: Trans-arterial chemo-embolisation (TACE)
items: Chemotherapy (e.g. doxorubicin) with Gelfoam or Lipiodol injected into the **hepatic artery**, which supplies the tumour
In unresectable HCC with good liver function: **60% 2-year survival vs 20% untreated**, but the gain is gone by 4 years
**Contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis** (Davidson also lists multifocal HCC)
Now mostly a **holding treatment** while definitive care is planned
Radioembolisation / selective internal radiation therapy (SIRT) is another arterial option

blocks.title: Systemic therapy
items: HCC is **not radiosensitive**, and IV chemotherapy (doxorubicin) gives only about a 30% response: a very limited role
**Sorafenib**: multikinase inhibitor (Raf, VEGF, PDGF); **the first systemic drug to prolong survival** (7.9 → 10.7 months)
**Lenvatinib**: alternative first-line tyrosine kinase inhibitor; **regorafenib** is also licensed
**Immunotherapy** (Pocket Medicine 8e): **atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1) + bevacizumab** preferred first-line; second line a kinase inhibitor or PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor

blocks.text: **Supportive care**: in the terminal stage (performance status > 2 or Child–Pugh C), treatment is best supportive care, and median survival is under 3 months. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy are used only in selected palliative settings or trials.

**Systemic therapy has moved on.** Davidson 24e names only sorafenib for advanced HCC. Pocket Medicine 8e makes **atezolizumab + bevacizumab first-line**, with kinase inhibitors second-line. For a Davidson-based question, answer sorafenib for the advanced stage, but know the immunotherapy combination.

cards.front: What proportion of HCC patients have underlying cirrhosis?
Annual HCC risk in chronic hepatitis B without vs with cirrhosis?
cards.back: 0.4% per year without cirrhosis; 2–6% per year with cirrhosis (about 4× higher if HBeAg-positive)

cards.front: Why can hepatitis B cause HCC without cirrhosis?
cards.back: HBV integrates its DNA into the hepatocyte genome

cards.front: Which fungus produces aflatoxin, and what food does it contaminate?
Leading cause of death in haemochromatosis with cirrhosis?
cards.back: HCC (about one-third); venesection lowers but does not remove the risk

cards.front: Two main routes by which HCC presents?
cards.back: Decompensation of (known or hidden) cirrhosis, usually incurable; or detection on surveillance, often curable

cards.front: Name three paraneoplastic features of HCC.
cards.back: Any three of: erythrocytosis, hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, thrombocytosis, carcinoid syndrome

cards.front: AFP level that warrants an aggressive search for HCC (no hepatitis flare)?
cards.back: > 400 ng/mL (330 IU/mL), or a steadily rising AFP; normal is < 10 ng/mL

cards.front: Non-malignant causes of a raised AFP?
cards.back: Active HBV/HCV replication; acute hepatic necrosis such as paracetamol overdose (very high)

cards.front: HCC surveillance test and interval?
cards.back: Ultrasound + AFP every 6 months in high-risk patients fit for treatment (cirrhosis, or chronic HBV even without cirrhosis)

cards.front: Classic HCC pattern on multiphase CT/MRI?
cards.back: Arterial-phase enhancement (hypervascular) followed by washout on portal venous/delayed phases

cards.front: Main reason to avoid biopsy in a transplant or resection candidate?
Feature on CT/MRI that separates FNH from hepatic adenoma?
Fibrolamellar HCC: typical patient and AFP?
cards.back: Young adult of either sex, no HBV or cirrhosis; AFP usually normal; resection gives about two-thirds 5-year survival

cards.front: Commonest biochemical abnormality with liver metastases?
Milan criteria for transplantation in HCC?
cards.back: One tumour < 5 cm, or up to three tumours each < 3 cm, with no vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread; about 75% 5-year survival

cards.front: Who is a candidate for resection if they have cirrhosis?
cards.back: Small tumour, Child–Pugh A, no portal hypertension

cards.front: Sorafenib: mechanism and benefit?
cards.back: Multikinase inhibitor (Raf, VEGF, PDGF); first systemic drug to prolong survival in HCC (7.9 → 10.7 months)

cards.front: Main contraindication to TACE?
cards.back: Decompensated cirrhosis (Davidson also lists multifocal HCC)

cards.front: Cure rate of percutaneous ethanol injection for HCC ≤ 3 cm?

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man who grew up in Taiwan has a 4 cm liver mass on ultrasound. His mother was a long-term carrier of a blood-borne virus. A biopsy taken during resection shows HCC in a liver with **no cirrhosis**. He is HBeAg-positive.
items.explanation: HBV is the cause that can produce HCC **without cirrhosis**, because viral DNA integrates into the host genome. Perinatal transmission (carrier mother) and HBeAg positivity (about 4× higher risk) fit. HCV-related HCC arises on a cirrhotic liver.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man has diabetes, bronze skin pigmentation and arthropathy of the second and third MCP joints. Transferrin saturation was very high when he was diagnosed with cirrhosis 8 years ago; weekly venesection normalised his ferritin. Surveillance ultrasound now shows a 3 cm lesion.
items.explanation: Diabetes, pigmentation and MCP arthropathy with iron overload point to **hereditary haemochromatosis**. In haemochromatosis with cirrhosis, HCC is the main cause of death and affects about one-third of patients; venesection lowers but does not remove the risk.

items.stem: A 48-year-old farmer from rural West Africa has no history of alcohol use and tests negative for hepatitis viruses. For years his family has eaten groundnuts stored in damp, mouldy conditions. He now has weight loss and a hard, irregular liver.
items.explanation: Mouldy groundnuts point to **aflatoxin**, a carcinogenic metabolite of _Aspergillus flavus_. It is the classic environmental cause of HCC.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has been stable and abstinent for 4 years. Over 6 weeks he has developed increasing ascites, a 6 kg weight loss and a constant ache under the right ribs. The liver edge is hard, irregular and tender, and a bruit is heard over it. Temperature is 37.8 °C.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of his deterioration?
questions.explanation: Rapid decompensation in a cirrhotic patient, with weight loss, RUQ pain and an **irregular tender liver with a bruit** (a hypervascular tumour), is classic HCC. Low-grade fever also occurs.
whyNot: SBP causes fever and abdominal pain but not weight loss, an irregular hard liver or a hepatic bruit.
He has been abstinent for 4 years, and alcoholic hepatitis does not cause an irregular mass with a bruit.
Haemangiomas are usually small and asymptomatic and do not cause decompensation.
Adenomas occur mainly in young women on the pill, not in older cirrhotic men.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with hepatitis C cirrhosis has a 5 cm liver mass and a raised AFP. His haemoglobin is 192 g/L with a raised haematocrit. He does not smoke, oxygen saturation is normal and he is not dehydrated.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation for the high haemoglobin?
questions.explanation: HCC is one of the classic tumours (with renal cell carcinoma and cerebellar haemangioblastoma) that cause **paraneoplastic erythrocytosis**. Other paraneoplastic features: hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypercholesterolaemia.
whyNot: A primary marrow disorder is less likely when a known tumour explains the finding.
Normal saturation and no smoking make hypoxic secondary polycythaemia unlikely.
He is clinically euvolaemic, so this is not relative polycythaemia.
Nothing in the history suggests androgen use.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with NASH cirrhosis attends routine surveillance. Ultrasound shows a new 1.8 cm nodule. Her serum AFP is 6 ng/mL (normal < 10).
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: HCC is still possible; characterise the nodule with multiphase CT or MRI
HCC is excluded because the AFP is normal
The nodule is a haemangioma because the AFP is normal
Repeat AFP in 12 months before any imaging
A normal AFP means only fibrolamellar HCC is possible
questions.explanation: AFP rises with tumour size, so **small screen-detected HCCs often have a normal AFP**. Kumar notes AFP is normal in at least a third of patients. A new nodule in cirrhosis needs multiphase CT/MRI.
whyNot: AFP has low sensitivity; a normal level does not exclude HCC.
AFP cannot tell lesion types apart; imaging characterises the nodule.
Waiting a year delays diagnosis of a possibly curable small tumour.
Fibrolamellar HCC occurs in young people without cirrhosis; this does not fit.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with hepatitis B cirrhosis has stable transaminases and an undetectable HBV DNA on antiviral treatment. His AFP has risen on three consecutive surveillance visits.
questions.leadIn: Above which AFP value (with no hepatitis flare) does Davidson recommend an aggressive search for HCC?
questions.explanation: Davidson: without a marked hepatitis flare, an AFP **> 400 ng/mL (330 IU/mL)** or a steadily rising AFP warrants an aggressive search for HCC. Normal is < 10 ng/mL. A progressive rise, as here, is itself a trigger.
whyNot: 10 ng/mL is the upper limit of normal, not the action threshold.
Not the threshold Davidson gives.
Not the threshold Davidson gives.
Far higher than the threshold; waiting for this level would delay diagnosis.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis on surveillance has a new 3 cm nodule on ultrasound. Her AFP is 35 ng/mL.
items.explanation: A new lesion found on screening ultrasound needs a **second modality: multiphase CT or MRI**. Arterial enhancement with washout confirms HCC without biopsy.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with compensated hepatitis C cirrhosis (Child–Pugh A) is well and would be fit for any treatment. He has never had liver cancer screening.
items.explanation: He has cirrhosis and is fit for treatment, so he needs **surveillance: ultrasound plus AFP every 6 months**.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with no history of liver disease, normal liver stiffness and negative hepatitis B and C serology has a 9 cm solitary liver mass. CT and MRI are not typical of HCC, and AFP is normal. No primary tumour is found elsewhere.
items.explanation: For a **large tumour in a patient without cirrhosis or HBV**, Davidson advises histology to confirm HCC and exclude a metastasis. Two-step reasoning: no cirrhosis, so imaging rules for cirrhotic livers do not apply.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman who has taken the combined oral contraceptive pill for 10 years has sudden severe RUQ pain and becomes hypotensive. CT shows a 6 cm liver lesion with blood in the peritoneum.
items.explanation: A young woman on the pill with a lesion that **ruptures and bleeds** is a **hepatic adenoma**. It needs resection (symptomatic and > 5 cm).

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has a 4 cm liver lesion found incidentally on ultrasound. MRI shows a well-defined lesion with a **central scar**. LFTs and AFP are normal.
items.explanation: A **central scar** separates FNH from adenoma. It is common in women under 40 and has no malignant potential.

items.stem: A 21-year-old man with no history of liver disease and negative hepatitis serology has a 12 cm liver mass. AFP is normal. Histology shows tumour cells set in dense bands of fibrous tissue.
items.explanation: **Fibrolamellar HCC**: young patient, no HBV or cirrhosis, large tumour, normal AFP, dense fibrous stroma. Resection gives a good prognosis.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man has lost 8 kg and has a change in bowel habit. CT shows numerous lesions scattered through both liver lobes. ALP is raised, while transaminases and AFP are normal.
items.explanation: **Multiple lesions** with a raised ALP and a likely bowel primary fit **metastases**, the commonest malignant liver tumours. GI primaries reach the liver via the portal vein.

questions.stem: Five patients with hepatitis C cirrhosis, no extrahepatic spread and no vascular invasion are discussed at a liver transplant meeting.
questions.leadIn: Which tumour burden falls within the Milan criteria?
options: Two tumours of 4 cm and 2 cm
A single 5.5 cm tumour with a 1 cm satellite
questions.explanation: Milan criteria: **one tumour < 5 cm, or up to three tumours each < 3 cm**, with vascular invasion and extrahepatic spread excluded. Three 2.5 cm nodules qualify. This gives about 75% 5-year survival after transplant.
whyNot: A single tumour must be < 5 cm.
With more than one tumour, each must be < 3 cm; the 4 cm lesion exceeds this.
More than three tumours is outside the criteria.
The main lesion is over 5 cm and there are two lesions.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with hepatitis C cirrhosis and a single 3 cm HCC is offered either resection or transplantation.
questions.leadIn: What is the main advantage of transplantation over resection for him?
options: It removes the cirrhotic liver, which cures the cirrhosis and the risk of new tumours
It removes any risk of hepatitis C recurring
It is suitable even with portal vein invasion
It does not require exclusion of extrahepatic spread
questions.explanation: Transplant **cures the underlying cirrhosis** and removes the risk of a second, de novo tumour. After resection the remaining cirrhotic liver can still grow new tumours (about 50% recurrence at 5 years).
whyNot: Transplant requires lifelong immunosuppression, which can speed up residual tumour.
Hepatitis C can recur in the graft and lead to cirrhosis and HCC again.
Vascular invasion must be excluded before transplant.
Extrahepatic disease must be excluded before transplant.

questions.theme: Treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma by stage
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man with Child–Pugh A cirrhosis and performance status 0 has **five HCC nodules** spread through both lobes. There is no vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread.
items.explanation: Multinodular disease with good liver function and PST 0 is **intermediate stage → TACE** (median survival about 20 months). This follows Davidson’s Fig. 22.36; note that Davidson’s text separately lists multifocal HCC among TACE contraindications, but the algorithm sends multinodular disease with preserved liver function to TACE.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman with Child–Pugh B cirrhosis has a 6 cm HCC with **tumour thrombus in the right portal vein**. She is up and about but cannot do heavy work (PST 1).
items.explanation: Portal vein invasion with PST 1–2 is **advanced stage → sorafenib** in Davidson’s algorithm (median survival about 11 months).

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with Child–Pugh C cirrhosis, gross ascites and confusion spends most of the day in bed (PST 3). CT shows multifocal HCC.
items.explanation: PST > 2 and Child–Pugh C means **terminal stage → best supportive care**; median survival is under 3 months. TACE is contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis.

questions.theme: Causes of a raised serum alpha-fetoprotein
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Acute hepatic necrosis after paracetamol overdose
Flare of active hepatitis B replication

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has a painless firm testicular swelling. AFP is raised. Liver ultrasound is normal.
items.explanation: AFP is a marker for **non-seminomatous germ cell tumours** as well as HCC. The testicular mass and normal liver point here.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman is admitted 2 days after deliberately taking a large number of paracetamol tablets. ALT is 6000 U/L, INR is 3.1 and AFP is markedly raised. Ultrasound shows no focal lesion.
items.explanation: **Acute hepatic necrosis**, as after paracetamol overdose, can give very high AFP levels without any tumour.

items.stem: A 44-year-old HBV carrier has ALT 900 U/L and a very high HBV DNA. AFP is modestly raised. Multiphase CT shows no focal lesion and no cirrhosis.
items.explanation: Active **HBV/HCV replication** raises AFP. This is why Davidson says to interpret AFP in the absence of a marked hepatitis flare.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with hepatitis B cirrhosis on suppressive antiviral treatment has normal transaminases. His AFP has climbed from 15 to 650 ng/mL over a year.
items.explanation: Two steps: the virus is suppressed and transaminases are normal (no flare), so a **steadily rising AFP > 400 ng/mL** in cirrhosis means HCC until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man born in South-east Asia has chronic hepatitis B. A 3 cm HCC is found. The surrounding liver shows no cirrhosis on histology.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism best explains HCC developing without cirrhosis?
options: Integration of viral DNA into the hepatocyte genome
questions.explanation: HBV DNA **integrates into the host hepatocyte genome**, which explains why HBV (unlike HCV) can cause HCC in a non-cirrhotic liver. Only about 30% of HCC patients in Taiwan have cirrhosis, compared with 90% in northern Europe.
whyNot: Iron overload is the mechanism in haemochromatosis, which acts mainly through cirrhosis.
Nothing suggests alcohol, and alcohol-related HCC arises on cirrhosis.
Not a recognised mechanism of HBV carcinogenesis.
Oestrogen is linked to hepatic adenoma, not HBV-related HCC.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with Child–Pugh A cirrhosis has a single 3.5 cm liver lesion. It enhances in the arterial phase and washes out on delayed phases on both CT and MRI. She is being assessed for liver transplantation. A junior doctor suggests a biopsy to be certain.
questions.leadIn: What is the main reason to avoid biopsy?
options: Risk of seeding tumour along the needle tract
Biopsy cannot distinguish HCC from normal liver
Biopsy is always falsely negative in HCC
questions.explanation: In possible transplant or resection candidates, Davidson advises **avoiding biopsy because of needle-tract seeding** (< 2%). Two concordant imaging modalities showing the typical pattern are enough for diagnosis.
whyNot: Well-differentiated HCC can be hard to tell from normal liver, but histology is usually diagnostic.
Biopsy does not usually precipitate encephalopathy.
Biopsy uses no contrast.
Sampling error causes some false negatives, but not always.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with known HCC and cirrhosis is now jaundiced with tense ascites (Child–Pugh C). CT shows two lesions without vascular invasion. The team discusses trans-arterial chemo-embolisation.
questions.leadIn: Which feature of his case most clearly contraindicates TACE?
questions.explanation: Davidson: TACE is **contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis**. Embolisation would further damage a failing liver. Jaundice and ascites (Child–Pugh C) mean decompensation.
whyNot: Age alone is not a contraindication.
AFP level does not determine TACE suitability.
Absence of vascular invasion is favourable, not a contraindication.
The cause of cirrhosis does not determine TACE eligibility.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with compensated hepatitis B cirrhosis asks how she will be monitored for liver cancer.
questions.leadIn: Which surveillance strategy is recommended?
questions.explanation: High-risk patients who would be fit for treatment have **ultrasound plus AFP every 6 months**. A new lesion or rising AFP leads to multiphase CT/MRI.
whyNot: CT is used to characterise lesions, not for routine surveillance, and 2 years is too long.
AFP alone misses many tumours because of its low sensitivity.
Biopsy is not a surveillance tool and has risks.
Far too infrequent to catch tumours early.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with hepatitis C cirrhosis has a new 2.8 cm nodule on surveillance ultrasound. He has multiphase contrast CT.
questions.leadIn: Which CT pattern would confirm HCC without the need for biopsy?
options: Arterial-phase enhancement with washout on portal venous and delayed phases
Peripheral nodular enhancement that slowly fills in towards the centre
A lesion with a central stellate scar
A non-enhancing lesion of fluid density
Rim enhancement around a low-density centre
questions.explanation: Step 1: HCC takes its blood supply from the **hepatic artery**, so it lights up in the arterial phase (hypervascular). Step 2: it then **washes out** on portal venous and delayed phases, compared with the surrounding liver. Step 3: in a high-risk (cirrhotic) patient, this pattern on multiphase CT or MRI establishes HCC **without biopsy**. Davidson recommends using two modalities: here, ultrasound then CT.
whyNot: Slow centripetal filling is the pattern of a haemangioma (delayed arterial filling).
A central scar suggests focal nodular hyperplasia.
A non-enhancing fluid-density lesion is a simple cyst.
Rim enhancement around a low-density centre suggests a metastasis or abscess, not classic HCC.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has Child–Pugh A cirrhosis and performance status 0. CT shows three HCC nodules of 1.5, 2 and 2.5 cm. There is no vascular invasion or extrahepatic disease, and she has no other significant illness.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson’s stage-based algorithm, which treatment is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Step 1, staging: Child–Pugh A and PST 0 with **three nodules each < 3 cm** is **early stage**, which is within the Milan criteria. Step 2: in the algorithm, three nodules go down the "associated diseases" branch, not the portal-pressure branch used for single tumours. Step 3: with **no other illness → liver transplantation**. With significant comorbidity it would be RFA/PEI. Transplant also cures the cirrhosis that would breed new tumours.
whyNot: Resection in the algorithm is for a single tumour with normal portal pressure; multiple nodules in a cirrhotic liver favour transplant.
TACE is for intermediate (multinodular beyond early criteria) disease, not for curable early-stage disease.
Sorafenib is for advanced disease (portal invasion, N1/M1, PST 1–2).
Supportive care is for terminal disease (PST > 2, Child–Pugh C).

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with hereditary haemochromatosis and cirrhosis has had venesection for 3 years, and his ferritin is now normal. He asks whether he can stop his 6-monthly liver scans.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate advice about HCC surveillance?
options: Stop now that ferritin is normal
Switch to AFP alone once a year
Surveillance is unnecessary because only viral cirrhosis causes HCC
questions.explanation: Step 1: cirrhosis is established, and it does not reverse when iron is removed. Step 2: in haemochromatosis with cirrhosis, HCC is the **main cause of death** (about one-third of patients). Step 3: **venesection lowers but does not abolish** that risk, so 6-monthly ultrasound plus AFP must continue.
whyNot: Normal ferritin does not remove the HCC risk once cirrhosis is present.
There is no time limit; the risk persists.
AFP alone is too insensitive for surveillance.
Haemochromatosis cirrhosis is a recognised HCC risk.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has been stable for years. Over 2 months he has developed rapidly increasing ascites, anorexia and a dull RUQ ache. AFP is 820 ng/mL.
items.explanation: Rapid decompensation in cirrhosis with a very high AFP is classic **HCC**.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman has a 2 cm liver lesion found incidentally on an ultrasound for gallstones. Contrast CT shows a low-density lesion with **delayed arterial filling**. She is well.
items.explanation: Low density with delayed filling on CT in an asymptomatic patient is a **haemangioma**, the commonest benign liver tumour. It needs no treatment and should not be biopsied.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man with ulcerative colitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis develops jaundice, rigors and a liver mass. AFP is normal and CA19-9 is raised.
items.explanation: PSC with IBD, cholangitis, jaundice, a raised CA19-9 and a normal AFP points to **cholangiocarcinoma**, which is not linked to cirrhosis or HBV.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with hypertension and bilaterally enlarged, cystic kidneys on ultrasound is also found to have many thin-walled fluid-filled lesions throughout the liver. LFTs are normal.
items.explanation: Multiple liver cysts together with renal cysts suggest **polycystic disease**. They are benign and need treatment only for mass effect.

questions.theme: Choosing a treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man with no liver disease and negative hepatitis serology has a single 8 cm HCC confined to the right lobe. Liver function is normal and he is fully active.
items.explanation: With **no cirrhosis, resection is the treatment of choice** (about 50% 5-year survival). Transplant criteria and the cirrhosis algorithm do not apply.

items.stem: A 56-year-old woman with Child–Pugh A hepatitis C cirrhosis and PST 0 has a single 4 cm HCC. Her hepatic venous pressure gradient is raised and she has small varices. She has no other illness.
items.explanation: Two steps: a single tumour < 5 cm is early stage, but **raised portal pressure rules out resection**. With no other illness, **transplantation** follows (within Milan criteria).

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with Child–Pugh A cirrhosis and PST 0 has a single 1.8 cm HCC and raised portal pressure. Severe ischaemic cardiomyopathy rules out major surgery.
items.explanation: A very early tumour with raised portal pressure **and significant comorbidity** leads to **RFA or ethanol injection**. Ethanol injection cures about 80% of tumours ≤ 3 cm.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with Child–Pugh A cirrhosis has HCC with portal vein invasion. His oncologist starts an oral drug and explains that it blocks several signalling enzymes, including Raf and the receptors for VEGF and PDGF.
questions.leadIn: Which drug has been started?
questions.explanation: **Sorafenib** is an oral multikinase inhibitor acting on Raf, VEGF and PDGF signalling. It was the first systemic drug to prolong survival in HCC (7.9 → 10.7 months). Lenvatinib and regorafenib are other kinase inhibitors.
whyNot: Doxorubicin is an anthracycline cytotoxic used in TACE, not a kinase inhibitor.
Bevacizumab is an anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody given intravenously, not an oral kinase inhibitor.
Atezolizumab is an anti-PD-L1 checkpoint antibody.
Tamoxifen is a hormonal agent with no role in HCC.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with advanced HCC is reviewed in clinic. His oncologist, following Pocket Medicine 8e, recommends first-line systemic treatment that combines a checkpoint inhibitor with an antiangiogenic antibody.
questions.leadIn: Which combination is this?
questions.explanation: Pocket Medicine 8e prefers **atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1) plus bevacizumab (anti-VEGF)** first-line, with a kinase inhibitor or PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor second-line. Davidson 24e, which is older, names only sorafenib.
whyNot: Both are kinase inhibitors; neither is a checkpoint inhibitor, and they are not combined.
This is the content of a chemo-embolisation, not systemic immunotherapy.
Two kinase inhibitors, not an immunotherapy combination.
Components of TACE, given into the hepatic artery.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman treated for breast cancer 3 years ago has an enlarged liver. CT shows multiple filling defects in both lobes. Transaminases and bilirubin are normal.
questions.leadIn: Which blood test is most likely to be abnormal?
questions.explanation: With liver metastases, a **raised ALP is the commonest biochemical abnormality**; Kumar says it is almost always raised. Other LFTs may be normal.
whyNot: AFP is a marker of HCC and germ cell tumours, not of breast metastases.
Transaminases are often normal with metastases, as here.
Albumin usually stays normal until disease is extensive.
Synthetic function is usually preserved.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman with no history of liver disease has a 10 cm mass in the left lobe of the liver. Hepatitis serology is negative, AFP is normal and imaging shows no cirrhosis or metastases. Histology shows malignant hepatocytes within dense fibrous stroma.
questions.leadIn: What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: This is **fibrolamellar HCC**. Its treatment of choice is **surgical resection**, after which about two-thirds of patients survive more than 5 years, a better outlook than ordinary HCC of the same size.
whyNot: Systemic therapy is for advanced unresectable disease; this tumour is resectable.
TACE is a holding or palliative option, not curative here.
Ethanol injection works for tumours ≤ 3 cm; this one is 10 cm.
A fit young patient with a resectable tumour needs curative treatment.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with hepatitis B cirrhosis has a 7 cm HCC. Doppler ultrasound shows a filling defect in the main portal vein.
questions.leadIn: This finding reflects the typical route by which HCC spreads. Which route is it?
options: Direct invasion into the portal vein and its branches
Spread along the bile ducts to the duodenum
Haematogenous spread to the brain first
Lymphatic spread to supraclavicular nodes first
questions.explanation: HCC takes its blood supply from the hepatic artery and characteristically **spreads by invading the portal vein** and its radicals. Portal invasion marks advanced disease and excludes transplantation.
whyNot: Peritoneal dissemination is more typical of metastatic adenocarcinoma.
Biliary spread is not the typical route.
Brain metastases are not characteristic.
Davidson notes nodal spread is common, but the typical vascular route is portal invasion.

questions.stem: Five patients with chronic hepatitis B are reviewed in a liver clinic.
questions.leadIn: Which patient has the highest annual risk of developing HCC?
questions.explanation: In chronic HBV, annual HCC risk is about **0.4% without cirrhosis and 2–6% with cirrhosis**. Risk is about **4× higher if HBeAg-positive**, and is higher in men and with age. Cirrhosis plus HBeAg positivity carries the highest risk.
whyNot: Cirrhosis raises risk, but HBeAg-negative status lowers it compared with option A.
Being HBeAg-positive raises risk, but without cirrhosis the annual risk is far lower.
Without cirrhosis the annual risk is far lower, and risk is lower in women than men.
No cirrhosis, HBeAg-negative and female: the lowest risk of these.

questions.theme: Next step in managing a liver lesion
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Stop the combined oral contraceptive pill and re-image

items.stem: A 40-year-old man from West Africa has chronic hepatitis B and is HBeAg-positive. Liver elastography and imaging show **no cirrhosis**. He is well and has never been screened for liver cancer.
items.explanation: Chronic HBV carries HCC risk **even without cirrhosis**, so screening with **6-monthly ultrasound and AFP** is indicated.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman who has taken the combined pill for 8 years has an asymptomatic 4 cm hepatic adenoma on MRI.
items.explanation: Kumar: resect an adenoma only if it is symptomatic, > 5 cm, or does not shrink after the pill is stopped. This one is asymptomatic and < 5 cm, so the first step is to **stop the pill and re-image**.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man with Child–Pugh A hepatitis C cirrhosis and portal hypertension has a single 3.5 cm lesion with arterial enhancement and washout on both CT and MRI. There is no vascular invasion or spread.
items.explanation: Two concordant modalities make the diagnosis, so biopsy is unnecessary and risks seeding. HCC < 5 cm in cirrhosis is an indication for **transplant assessment**; portal hypertension rules out resection.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is assessed for liver transplantation for HCC.
questions.leadIn: Which finding would exclude him from transplantation for HCC?
options: Tumour invasion of a major branch of the portal vein
Three tumours each 2 cm in diameter
questions.explanation: Transplant assessment focuses on **excluding vascular invasion and extrahepatic spread**. The UK criteria require **no macrovascular invasion or metastases**. Options B and C are within the Milan criteria.
whyNot: A single tumour < 5 cm is within the Milan criteria.
Up to three tumours each < 3 cm is within the Milan criteria.
AFP is not part of the size or vascular-invasion criteria quoted.
Portal hypertension does not exclude transplantation; it is a reason to prefer it over resection.

ospe.identify: Contrast CT: a large hepatocellular carcinoma (arrows) in the liver → HCC
Multiphase CT/MRI: bright lesion in the arterial phase that washes out on portal venous and delayed phases → classic HCC
H&E histology: malignant cells resembling hepatocytes → hepatocellular carcinoma
CT: multiple scattered liver lesions (arrows) → liver metastases
MRI: well-defined benign liver lesion (arrows) → haemangioma, the commonest benign liver tumour
CT: many cysts in both the liver and kidneys → polycystic disease
